chapter.name: Another Peek Beyond the Point
chapter.blurb: Multiplying and dividing decimals: place value and powers of ten, decimal multiplication and the size of products, division by counting numbers and by decimals, quotients that never end, and the leap year calendar.

scope: Recall decimals as fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000, write a fraction as a sum of tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and divide by 10, 100, 1000 by moving the decimal point
Multiply a decimal by a counting number and by another decimal by converting to fractions
Multiply decimals by removing the decimal points, multiplying, and placing the point using the total number of decimal places
Decide whether a product is greater or less than the numbers multiplied, and use a known product to write related products
Multiply decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 and solve word problems with decimal multiplication
Divide a decimal by 10, 100, 1000, and write a division of counting numbers as a decimal using an equivalent fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000
Divide by counting numbers with long division using place value, regrouping into tenths, hundredths and thousandths, including decimal dividends
Divide by a decimal by multiplying the divisor and dividend by the same power of ten, and compare the quotient with the dividend
Recognise decimal quotients that never end, such as 10 divided by 3 and 1 divided by 7, and explain why the remainders repeat
Explain the leap year rules using decimal multiplication, and count days over 100 and 1000 calendar years
Recurring decimals written with bar notation and converting them back to fractions -- the chapter only shows that the digits repeat
Rounding or estimating decimals to a given number of places -- not taught in this chapter
Cyclic numbers such as 142857 as a proof topic and Artin's conjecture -- mentioned only as a curiosity
The Hidato puzzle -- recreational puzzle not linked to a concept

concepts.name: Decimals as fractions, and multiplying or dividing by 10, 100, 1000
concepts.description: Reading decimals as fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000, expanding them by place value, and multiplying or dividing by powers of ten by moving the decimal point.
concepts.idea: A decimal is a fraction with denominator 10, 100, 1000, so multiplying or dividing by a power of ten shifts every digit that many places.
concepts.rule: Dividing by 10, 100, 1000 moves the decimal point left by the number of zeroes, adding zeroes in front if needed; multiplying moves it right.

concepts.name: Multiplying decimals
concepts.description: Multiplying a decimal by a counting number or by another decimal, using fractions and the rule for placing the decimal point.
concepts.idea: Multiplying decimals is multiplying their fractions, so the numerators multiply and the denominators multiply to a power of ten.
concepts.rule: Remove the decimal points, multiply as counting numbers, and give the product as many decimal places as the two numbers have together.

concepts.name: Size of a product and using a known product
concepts.description: Deciding whether a product is greater or less than the numbers multiplied and using one known product to write related products by moving the decimal point.
concepts.idea: Multiplying by a number greater than 1 makes bigger and by a number between 0 and 1 makes smaller, just as with fractions.
concepts.rule: Both numbers above 1: product larger than both; both between 0 and 1: product smaller than both; one of each: product between them. Related products differ only in the decimal point.

concepts.name: Dividing decimals by counting numbers
concepts.description: Dividing by counting numbers with an equivalent fraction with denominator 10, 100, 1000, and with long division that regroups into tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
concepts.idea: When ones remain they can be regrouped into tenths, then hundredths, so a division of counting numbers can continue into decimal places.
concepts.rule: Regroup the remainder into the next smaller place, put the decimal point in the quotient when moving from ones to tenths, and stop when the remainder is 0.

concepts.name: Dividing by a decimal
concepts.description: Dividing by a decimal divisor by turning it into a counting number, and comparing the quotient with the dividend.
concepts.idea: Multiplying the divisor and the dividend by the same power of ten leaves the quotient unchanged.
concepts.rule: Multiply divisor and dividend by 10, 100, ... until the divisor is a counting number, then divide; dividing by a number below 1 gives a quotient greater than the dividend.

concepts.name: Decimal quotients that never end
concepts.description: Recognising divisions such as 10 by 3 and 1 by 7 whose decimals never end and explaining why the remainders and digits repeat.
concepts.idea: If a remainder repeats in long division, the same steps repeat forever, so the digits of the quotient repeat in a cycle.
concepts.rule: Dividing by n leaves fewer than n different non-zero remainders, so either the division ends or a remainder repeats and the digits cycle.

concepts.name: Leap years and the calendar
concepts.description: Explaining the leap year rules with decimal multiplication and counting calendar days over 100 and 1000 years.
concepts.idea: The Earth takes 365.2422 days to go round the Sun, so extra days are added to the calendar and then some are taken back.
concepts.rule: A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which are leap years only if divisible by 400.
concepts.example: In 1000 years there are 242 leap years, giving 750 x 365 + 240 x 366 + 8 x 365 + 2 x 366 = 365,242 days.
